Teacher Guide & What's Inside

About This Resource

This no-prep set helps third graders see fractions as numbers on a number line. Students partition 0 to 1 into equal parts, then name and place unit fractions and fractions a/b, including fractions greater than 1. They also find equivalent fractions and whole numbers at the same point. Every page uses one simple story: Juniper the snowshoe hare hops from Base Camp (0) to the Cocoa Cabin (1), and every hop on a trail is the same size.

The Trail Routine (use it every day)

  1. Count the hops. How many equal parts (intervals) are there from 0 to 1? That number is the denominator.
  2. Name one hop. Each hop is the unit fraction 1/b.
  3. Hop to the spot. Start at 0 and count hops. The number of hops is the numerator.

Always pair the trail word with the math word: “each hop (equal part),” “the cabin (1 whole).”

What the Paws Mean

Each student page has 1, 2, or 3 pairs of paw prints in the top corner. The paws let you group students without labels like “easy” or “hard.”

PawsLevelBest forWhat students do
1 pairBase CampNew learners, interventionUnit fractions on 0–1. Tick marks are given, and some hop arcs are drawn.
2 pairsTrailMost of the classAny fraction a/b on 0–1, plus some fractions greater than 1 on 0–2 lines.
3 pairsSummitStudents ready for a challengeEquivalent fractions, whole numbers as fractions, 0–3 lines, and written proof.

Differentiate fast: All three Trail Mazes use the same rules, so you can give directions once. Then hand out Maze 1 (Base Camp), Maze 2 (Trail), or Maze 3 (Summit). Pages 4 and 5 get harder as students go down the page, so Base Camp students may stop halfway. Pages 8, 10, and 11 include sentence frames for English learners and reluctant writers.

Early finishers: On the back of page 8, students design a “trick” trail sign for a friend to check.

Most pages take 15–25 minutes; the game takes about 20 minutes. Every page also works as a math center or small-group task.

Tips

  1. Keep the Trail Guide (p. 3) close. Students can keep a copy in a folder or post it as an anchor chart.
  2. “Count the hops, not the marks.” A line cut into 4 hops has 5 tick marks. This is the most common number line error, and every maze includes it as a trap.
  3. Mazes check themselves. Each Cocoa Cabin says how many footprints the right trail has. If a student hits a dead end or the count is wrong, they go back to the last sign they colored and re-check it. The answer key (p. 16) shows which mistake each wrong sign matches.
  4. Name the point with the line's hops. On a fourths line the answer is 2/4. Students do not need to rewrite fractions with smaller numbers, because that is not a grade 3 standard. If a student writes 1/2 and explains that it is the same point, accept it.

Printing Notes

  • Everything is black-and-white friendly and printed one-sided.
  • Only two things need cutting: the Trail Tickets (p. 14, four per page) and the Game Answer Card (p. 17, one per pair of players). Everything else is no prep.
  • The full text of each standard is on page 18.

Trail Guide: Fractions on a Number Line

Count the hops. Name one hop. Hop to the spot.

1Count the hops.
→ the denominator
There are 4 equal hops (equal parts) from 0 to 1. The denominator is 4.
2Name one hop.
→ the unit fraction
Each hop is 1/4 of the whole. 1/4 is a unit fraction.
3Hop to the spot.
→ the numerator
Start at 0. Juniper took 3 hops of 1/4. The numerator is 3. She is at 3/4.

Count the hops, not the marks!

0 is where Juniper starts. She has not hopped yet. 4 hops make 5 marks. Count the hops!

You reached the cabin!

4 hops of 1/4 reach the cabin. 4/4 = 1 whole.

Word Bank
number lineA line that shows numbers in order.
fractionA number that names equal parts of a whole.
numeratorThe top number. It counts hops from 0.
denominatorThe bottom number. Equal hops from 0 to 1.
equal partsParts that are all the same size.
unit fractionOne equal part, like 1/4.
wholeThe whole trail from 0 to 1.
tick markA short line that marks a spot.
intervalThe space between two tick marks. One hop!
equivalentEqual. Worth the same amount.
same pointOne spot on the line with two names.

How to play
  1. Pick an open square. Say the fraction.
  2. Your partner checks the Answer Card.

  4. Get 4 in a row across, down, or diagonal to win!
FFootprint: Name the footprint. Use the trail's hops.
TTwo trails: Name the bottom fraction at the same spot.
CCabin: The footprint is on a whole number. Name it as a fraction. Use the trail's hops.

If Students Stop Here…

When a student colors a false sign, its code tells you what they were thinking.

CodeWhat the student didExample sign in the mazesWhat it meansNext step
M1Counted tick marks, not hops4 hops, sign says 1/5 (Maze 1 R1C4); 3/5 (Maze 2 R2C3)Thinks the marks are the partsHave them draw hop arcs and count the arcs, not the marks.
M2Counted the tick at 0 as “1”point at 1/6, sign says 2/6 (Maze 1 R2C1); 3/8 → 4/8 (Maze 2 R4C3)Starts counting before the first hop“0 is where Juniper starts. She hasn't hopped yet.”
M3Flipped the numerator and denominator1/2 → 2/1 (Maze 1 R2C4); 4/8 → 8/4 (Maze 2 R2C2); 6/3 → 3/6 (Maze 3 R3C4)Unsure which number is whichReview: the bottom number is the number of hops in 1 whole.
M4Guessed the denominator from the looksixths line, sign says 1/8 (Maze 1 R2C2); 5/6 → 5/8 (Maze 2 R4C4)Did not count the hopsCount the hops every time, even when lines look alike.
M5Named one hop instead of the spotpoint at 3/4, sign says 1/4 (Maze 1 R3C4)Mixes up “size of one hop” and “where she landed”Ask: “How big is one hop? How many hops did she take?”
M6Used the whole 0–2 line as 1 wholepoint at 6/4, sign says 6/8 (Maze 2 R3C1)Thinks the whole is the full linePoint to the cabin at 1: “The whole is 0 to 1.”
M7Wrote the whole number as the numeratorpoint at 2 on fourths, sign says 2/4 (Maze 3 R2C3)Sees “2” and writes it on top“How many fourths does it take to reach Cabin 2?”
M8Same numerator = same spot1/3 and 1/6 (Maze 3 R1C3)Compares top numbers onlyStack the lines and check whether the points line up.
M9Same distance from 1 = equal2/3 and 5/6 (Maze 3 R2C1); 3/4 and 7/8 (Maze 3 R4C4)“Both are 1 hop from the cabin”Hops are different sizes. Compare where the points really are.

Answer Key: pp. 10–14 + Game Answer Card

Page 10 — Fix the Trail Sign

  1. Nadia: Needs a fix. The footprint is at 1/4. Sample: The mistake is she counted 5 tick marks. There are only 4 hops from 0 to 1. “Draw it right”: 4 equal hops with the dot at the end of the first hop, labeled 1/4.
  2. Emeka: Needs a fix. Sample: The mistake is the hops are not the same size, so they are not thirds. “Draw it right”: 3 equal hops with the dot at the end of the first hop, labeled 1/3.
  3. Lucia: Needs a fix. The footprint is at 2/6 (also accept 1/3 if the student explains it is the same point). Sample: The mistake is she counted the mark at 0 as 1. Juniper only took 2 hops.
  4. Tobias: Correct. Sample: I know because 2 hops of 1/4 and 4 hops of 1/8 both land halfway, on the same point.

Page 11 — Trail Talk

  1. Always. Sample proof: Split 0 to 1 into 2 hops, then into 4 hops. Each 1/4 hop is shorter than a 1/2 hop because the same whole is shared by more hops.
  2. Sometimes. Sample proof: 3/4 is less than 1. But 4/4 lands right on 1, and 5/4 is past 1.
  3. Sometimes. Sample proof: 1/2 and 2/4 land on the same spot. 1/3 and 1/4 do not; 1/3 is farther from 0.
  4. Never. Sample proof: 4 hops have 5 tick marks, because there is a mark at 0 before the first hop. There is always one more tick mark than hops.

Accept any correct number line proof.

Page 13 — Summit Check (1 point each)

  1. 6 hops; each hop is 1/6 (both parts needed)
  2. Dot at the first tick after 0 (1/3)
  3. 5/8
  4. Dot at the 4th tick after 0 (4/6)
  5. B. 2/8
  6. Yes (4/8 and 3/6 are both halfway)
  7. 6/6
  8. 4/2

Page 14 — Trail Tickets

  • A: Dot at the first tick after 0. Sample: There are 8 equal hops, and 1/8 is the end of the first hop.
  • B: 5/6. Sample: I counted 5 hops of 1/6 from 0.
  • C: 2/6. Sample: 2 hops of 1/6 land on the same spot as 1/3.
  • D: 3/3. Sample: 3 hops of 1/3 reach the cabin at 1.
Game Answer Card: Snowball Four-in-a-RowPrint one per pair. Two trails = the bottom fraction.

If a player says an equal fraction with the trail's hops, it is correct; the “also” answers are for players who explain the same spot.

Standards Alignment, Terms of Use & Credits

Common Core State Standards: Grade 3, Number & Operations—Fractions

3.NF.A — Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.

CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.3.NF.A.2 Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

  • 3.NF.A.2.A Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line. (pp. 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13, 14)
  • 3.NF.A.2.B Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line. (pp. 3, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14)

CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.3.NF.A.3 Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

  • 3.NF.A.3.A Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line. (pp. 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14)
  • 3.NF.A.3.B Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3. Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model. (pp. 8, 11)
  • 3.NF.A.3.C Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers. Examples: Express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6; locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram. (pp. 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14)
